tagline.text: A deep, round plunge pool in a Siniloan forest gorge, named for a vanished stone bridge

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Magsaysay, Siniloan, Laguna (below the Trekkers registration point at Km 17 of the Siniloan–Famy–Infanta Road)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~900 (per person, day trip from Manila)

children.text: Tulay na Bato Falls hides in a forested gorge in Siniloan, at the eastern edge of Laguna, with a deep round pool and big boulders around it. It can be done as a day trip from Manila by bus, as a guided trek on foot.

Tulay na Bato Falls lies in the hills of Barangay Magsaysay in the town of Siniloan, Laguna. Heading up the Siniloan–Famy–Infanta Road toward the Quezon border, you reach a registration point called Trekkers at the 17 km marker. Most visitors register there, get assigned a guide, and walk down through the forest to the falls. In Filipino, tulay means bridge and bato means stone, so the name literally means "Stone Bridge Falls."

The name comes from an old stone bridge. Many travel accounts say a stone bridge once stood near the falls, that a typhoon destroyed it, and that its remains can still be seen. One blog says it dates from the Japanese occupation, and guides reportedly point to a big boulder along the trail as part of the bridge. This origin comes from travelers' accounts and local guides rather than an official source, so treat it as local lore.

This is a place remembered for its pool and rocks rather than for sheer height. Sources disagree on the drop, ranging from about 9 m to 20 m, so it is hard to give a firm figure. Below the fall is a round pool said to be up to about 6 m (20 ft) deep at its deepest, followed by a short, wide cascade. On the left side of the falls is a sculpted rock wall with a big slab jutting out like a hammerhead, and the surroundings are ringed by house-sized boulders.

This is not a developed tourist site. Records say few people visit, so there is little trash collection or maintenance staff, and the trail is full of wet rocks and mud. In return you get a quiet gorge waterfall to hike to and swim in, half a day from Manila, which suits anyone who wants something calmer than a famous tourist waterfall such as Pagsanjan Falls. The usual plan is to combine it with Hagdang Bato Falls, further down the same gorge. If this is your first waterfall trek near Manila, plan realistically: accounts of the walk down from the registration point range from about 30 minutes to a little over an hour, and continuing to Hagdang Bato takes you past half a day. If you travel by public transport, plan to be back at the registration point by 3~4 PM so you do not miss a bus home, and bring a change of clothes because you will ride home damp. The falls themselves are not tall, so you may be let down if you expect a big waterfall. It suits people who enjoy boulders, pools and forest walking.
The pool below the falls is said to be as deep as about 6 m, and some people jump in from the rocks above. Guides sometimes discourage diving or canyoneering, so follow their instructions on site.
On the left of the falls is a smooth rock wall with a big slab jutting out like a hammerhead. The water-carved texture of the stone makes good photos.

blocks.title: Traces of the old stone bridge

children.text: The stone bridge that gave the falls its name was reportedly destroyed by a typhoon, and its remains can still be seen. Ask your guide, who will point out a big roadside boulder.

blocks.title: A forest trail through a coffee farm

children.text: The land around the Trekkers registration point is a private property of about 10 hectares, and part of the trail passes through a coffee plantation. You walk a cool dirt path under tall trees.
About 1 km downstream is Hagdang Bato Falls, where water spills down like stairs, and most visitors combine the two. It has several shallow pools that are good for splashing around.
It takes about 3 hours by bus from Manila to reach the registration point, so a day trip is possible if you leave early in the morning. Many accounts say no advance reservation is needed.

items.title: Day-trip route
items.subtitle: Tulay na Bato Falls and Hagdang Bato Falls

children.text: Take a bus bound for Infanta or Real from a Raymond bus terminal in Manila, such as the one in Legarda, on one of the early departures. Tell the driver in advance that you are getting off at "Trekkers."
Arrive at the Trekkers registration point, complete
registration and the orientation
, and get assigned a guide. Snacks and drinks are sold at the registration point, but it is better to bring your own.
Walk down the forest trail with your guide. It starts with a slippery descent, crosses a couple of small streams, and the last stretch goes over big boulders.
Arrive at Tulay na Bato Falls, swim in the pool and take photos. The rocks are wet, so do not rush.
Follow the gorge toward Hagdang Bato Falls for lunch and a swim. The current is noticeable in this section, so hold on to the rocks as you move.
Return to the area near Trekkers by a different trail. Wash up and change, then catch a bus back to Manila at around 4 PM.
This timetable is an example combined from several travel accounts. Actual times vary a lot with group size, weather and water level, so settle the plan with your local guide.

From Siniloan town, take a jeepney toward Infanta or a tricycle up to Magsaysay and get off at Trekkers. Accounts put the jeepney fare at a few tens of pesos.
If you drive, turn off Manila East Road onto the Siniloan–Famy–Infanta Road and look for Trekkers at about
17 km
. Typing "Trekkers" into a map app works.

Because this is a gorge waterfall, it is safest to avoid going during or right after rain. Travel accounts all say that in the rainy season the trail turns muddy, leeches are common, and the water rises dangerously.

The most reliable window is the drier months of March to May, which are also hot, so a swim is most welcome. The area can still get rain from December to February under the northeast monsoon, so check the weather before you go.

Going on a weekday keeps it quiet. Many accounts say it does not get very crowded even on weekends and holidays, but guide assignment can be slow if group visits overlap. Arrive early in the morning, swim first, and leave the falls before lunchtime.

A day trip is the usual way to visit Tulay na Bato Falls, so there is almost no lodging near the falls. Some accounts say the Trekkers registration point sells snacks and drinks, but the selection is limited, so bring your own packed lunch and water. If you want to camp, first confirm the rules and fees with the owner of the registration point and the barangay office.

For proper lodging and meals, it is easier to come down to Siniloan town. The town has restaurants and a market, and it is where vans and buses to Manila gather. You can also find places to eat near Famy Junction. Businesses change often, so check on site.

A packed lunch is the safest choice. Put rice and side dishes in a waterproof container and carry plenty of water. What the registration point sells depends on its stock that day, and there are no restaurants around the falls. A common plan is to come down to Siniloan town after the hike, eat at a local restaurant, and then take a van to Manila.
Leave early. Registration and travel take time, and late in the afternoon the last buses home get tight.
Bring a waterproof bag and water shoes (or sandals with good grip). There are many wet boulder sections and you cross streams several times.
Bring a change of clothes and a towel. You wash up and change near the registration point before heading home.
Keep your phone in a waterproof pouch. Mobile signal is weak in the hills, so download an offline map.
Some accounts recommend a bolo knife for overgrown sections, but it is safer to leave that to your guide than to carry one yourself.
Carry your trash out. Accounts say there is no one to collect it near the falls.
Accounts mention village kids who guide you along the trail for small tips. Settle that separately from the official guide.
If you plan to continue to Hagdang Bato, pace your energy and prepare lunch in advance.
Once your guide is assigned, decide first how far you will go today. Agreeing on whether to go on to Hagdang Bato and which trail to return by makes timing easier.
Sitting on a bus wet can get cold, so bring a light jacket and put your shoes and clothes in a separate plastic bag.
Do not go during rain or right after it. The rocks are slippery and the creek can rise suddenly.

A guide is practically mandatory. Travel accounts and reviews describe a "no guide, no hike" arrangement, and the trail has almost no signage, so register at the registration point and stay with your guide.
The last stretch is steep and slippery rock. Some descents have no roots or bushes to hold onto, so go down slowly.
The pool is deep, so weak swimmers should not enter without a life jacket. Check the depth and the rocks with your guide before jumping from above.
Several accounts say leeches are common in the rainy season. Bring long socks and insect repellent.
Fees, registration rules and trail conditions can change. Check the latest notices with the Siniloan tourism, culture and arts office before you go.
About
1 km
downstream in the same gorge, this stair-step waterfall is usually combined with Tulay na Bato. One account says the trail on this side is harder.
A small waterfall near Hagdang Bato with a small cave behind it, reportedly. Confirm the route with your guide.
You pass this waterfall on the road up to Trekkers, so you can spot where it is from the bus. It is close by, so you may be able to stop by depending on your schedule.
A 2016 account says access was blocked over an ownership jurisdiction issue. The current status is unknown, so ask a local guide whether it is open.
